title: Direct Memory Access
body:
The third and fastest answer to "how does data get between a device and memory", after
[[Programmed I-O]] and [[Interrupt Driven I-O]]. A **DMA controller** takes over the
[[System Bus]] and moves the data itself; the [[CPU]] never touches a single byte.

The escalation is worth seeing side by side:

| | CPU work per byte | Interruptions |
|---|---|---|
| [[Polling]] | Busy-wait, then move it | Continuous |
| [[Interrupt Driven I-O]] | Run an [[ISRs\|ISR]], then move it | One [[IRQs\|IRQ]] per byte |
| **DMA** | None | One [[IRQs\|IRQ]] per *transfer* |

**How a transfer goes.** The CPU programs the controller with a source address, a
destination address, and a count, then goes back to work. The controller requests the bus,
the CPU grants it and floats its own bus drivers (this is *cycle stealing*: the CPU stalls
only when it needs the bus in the same cycle), the controller moves the block, and when
the count hits zero it raises an interrupt to say it is done.

This is why disk and network transfers scale. Per-byte interrupt overhead at disk speeds
would swamp the processor entirely.

Two consequences worth carrying into [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: the DMA controller writes to
physical addresses, so the OS has to pin pages and translate addresses before handing them
over, and it writes behind the CPU's back, so caches have to be invalidated over the
affected range.
